topic: Henry Molaison: the man who could not make a new memory for 55 years
script:
Imagine meeting someone for the first time. You talk for twenty minutes. You laugh. You like them. Then they step out of the room for a moment, and when they walk back in, you have no idea who they are.

Now imagine that this happens with every person, every conversation, every single day, for the rest of your life.

For fifty-five years, that was the life of a man named Henry Molaison. For most of that time, the world only knew him by two letters: H.M. And without ever remembering it, he taught us more about the human memory than almost anyone who has ever lived.

Henry was born in 1926 in Connecticut. By most accounts, he was a normal, friendly kid. But in childhood, he started having seizures. Some people believe they may have been linked to a bicycle accident when he was young, but no one knows for sure.

As he grew older, the seizures got worse. By his twenties, they were happening so often that he could barely live a normal life. He had to drop out of school for a while. He struggled to hold down a job. Medication didn't help enough. His family was desperate.

So in 1953, when Henry was twenty-seven, they agreed to something drastic. A neurosurgeon in Hartford named William Scoville believed he could stop the seizures by removing the part of the brain where he thought they were starting.

The operation was experimental. Scoville removed a section deep inside both sides of Henry's brain, including most of a small, curved structure called the hippocampus. At the time, nobody really knew what the hippocampus did.

They were about to find out.

When Henry woke up, the good news was that his seizures were much better. His personality was the same. His intelligence was the same, in fact slightly above average. He could talk, joke, read, and remember his childhood.

But something was terribly wrong.

He couldn't find his way to the bathroom in the hospital. He didn't recognize the staff he had met the day before. He couldn't remember what he had eaten for lunch. Every few minutes, the world reset.

Henry had lost the ability to form new long-term memories. Doctors call this anterograde amnesia. He could hold a thought for a short time, especially if he kept repeating it to himself. But the moment his attention moved on, it was gone forever.

He could read the same magazine again and again, and it would feel brand new every time. He would be told that a family member had died, feel the full shock and grief, and then, later, ask where they were. Every time he learned it, it was the first time.

It's almost impossible to imagine. But Henry once described it in words that researchers recorded. He said that every day is alone in itself, whatever enjoyment he had had, and whatever sorrow.

In 1955, a young psychologist from Montreal named Brenda Milner came to study him. What she discovered would change neuroscience.

Before Henry, many scientists believed that memory was spread out across the whole brain, a bit everywhere. Henry's case showed that wasn't true. A specific part of the brain, the part that had been removed, was essential for turning new experiences into lasting memories. Without it, nothing new could stick.

But Milner's most famous experiment revealed something even stranger.

She gave Henry a simple task. He had to trace the outline of a star, but he could only see his hand and the paper in a mirror. If you've ever tried this, you know it's surprisingly hard. Everything is backwards. Your hand goes the wrong way.

On the first day, Henry made lots of mistakes, just like anyone would. On the second day, he did better. On the third day, he was even better, smooth and accurate.

But every single day, he had no memory of ever doing the task before. He was surprised at how well he was doing. As far as he knew, it was his very first try.

Think about what that means. His hands were learning. His brain was getting better at the skill. But he had no memory of the practice at all.

This proved that we don't have just one memory system. We have at least two. One for facts and events, like what you did yesterday or the name of the person you just met. And another for skills and habits, like riding a bike, typing, or tracing a star in a mirror. Henry had lost the first one. The second one still worked perfectly.

That discovery is now in every psychology textbook in the world.

Over the following decades, Henry became one of the most studied people in the history of science. Researchers tested his memory, his perception, his language, his sense of time. A neuroscientist named Suzanne Corkin worked with him for more than forty years. She knew him incredibly well. He never knew her at all. Every time she walked into the room, she was a pleasant stranger, though some researchers noticed he sometimes seemed to have a vague feeling that he'd met her before, perhaps at school.

To protect his privacy, scientists only ever called him H.M. Thousands of students learned about H.M. without knowing his name, his face, or the life he was living. And through all of it, by every account, Henry stayed cheerful, polite, and patient. He often said he hoped that what was learned from him would help other people.

As the years passed, Henry grew older. But in his own mind, in a sense, time had stopped somewhere in the early 1950s. When he looked in the mirror as an old man, the reflection didn't match the young man he still felt he was.

Henry Molaison died on December 2nd, 2008, at the age of eighty-two. Only then was his real name revealed to the world.

But his contribution wasn't finished. Henry had agreed to donate his brain to science. In 2009, at the University of California, San Diego, a team led by Jacopo Annese carefully cut his brain into two thousand, four hundred and one ultra-thin slices, each thinner than a millimeter. The process was streamed live on the internet, and people around the world watched. Those slices were scanned and turned into a detailed digital map, so that scientists anywhere could study the brain that changed our understanding of memory.

So what did we really learn from Henry?

We learned where new memories are made. We learned that memory comes in different kinds. We learned why surgeons should never remove that part of the brain on both sides, a lesson that has protected countless patients since. And research built on his case still shapes how we study conditions like Alzheimer's disease today.

There's something both sad and beautiful about his story. Henry Molaison couldn't remember a single scientist who studied him, not one of the thousands of tests he took, not a single moment of the fame he had as H.M.

But the rest of us will remember him.

If you found this story fascinating, subscribe for more of the strangest and most human stories in science. And tell me in the comments, if you could only keep one kind of memory, facts or skills, which would you choose?

youtube.title: He Couldn't Make a New Memory for 55 Years - and Changed Science Forever
youtube.description:
In 1953, an experimental brain surgery stopped Henry Molaison's seizures - and left him unable to form a single new memory for the rest of his life.

Known to science only as 'H.M.', Henry became one of the most studied people in history. A simple mirror-drawing test proved that we have more than one kind of memory, and his brain - cut into 2,401 slices after his death - is still teaching scientists today.

This is the true story of the man who could never remember the people who studied him, and the world that will never forget him.

Subscribe for more of the strangest and most human stories in science.

facebook.text: After a brain surgery in 1953, Henry Molaison could never form a new memory again - every person he met was a stranger, every day. Yet his hands could still learn new skills he had no memory of practising. His case changed neuroscience forever. If you could only keep one kind of memory - facts or skills - which would you choose?
